source.title: Brevity Constraints Reverse Performance Hierarchies in Language Models

record.file_problem: The text contains the main paper and substantial appendices, but appears to end abruptly in Appendix B.2.6 after an equation; the remainder, if any, is not present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy across model sizes and prompt conditions, testing scale-related downstream performance with a different measure from held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own downstream accuracy results by model size and tests prompt interventions, so these bear on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit loss power laws, test large-run loss extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its statements about architecture independence concern inverse-scaling accuracy patterns, not whether depth or width changes loss only slightly. Scaling-law findings mentioned in related work are citations, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: Across 31 models (0.5B–405B) on 1,485 problems from five benchmarks, the study measures per-problem accuracy by size and argues that downstream scaling (V6) needs restating: about 7.7% of problems show small models beating large ones, and prompt choice changes the size gap. These are its own results on downstream performance versus scale. The headline reversal numbers, however, come from a subset selected for being reversed.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also state that aggregate scaling laws predict trends under fixed prompts, and that large models have latent capability masked by universal prompting. Note that they do not test the post-hoc selection of the inverse subset.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream benchmark accuracy across model sizes and prompt conditions; it does not use the original scaling-law loss measurement or fit power-law loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt condition and dataset change the size-performance gap; the study reports a BoolQ gap increase under brevity and gap reversals on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM.

fits_no_version.finding: Large models produce longer responses (median 197 tokens), and brevity prompts cut length 60% while changing accuracy on the selected items.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale-dependent verbosity under bare prompts affects downstream accuracy measurement.

record.problems: The study uses greedy decoding and five benchmarks; intervention results cover selected models, and the text says the selected models have a larger control gap than the full analysis. The paired intervention test uses 96 problems despite the described intervention on 115 inverse-scaling problems. Reported inverse-problem aggregate accuracies conflict between Section 4.2 and Appendix A.4.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results left out. Architecture-family comparisons are not extracted as V4 rows because they do not isolate depth or width at fixed parameter count or measure loss.

untested.parts: Aggregate benchmark accuracy versus size across all 1,485 problems is not reported. There is no prediction from pretraining loss and no fitted scaling trend.
All; no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: the family comparisons do not hold parameter count fixed and do not measure loss.

missing.what: Problem categorisation over all 1,485 problems: 48.1% normal scaling, 7.7% inverse, 17.3% ceiling, 9.8% floor. This is the only unselected size-versus-accuracy result.
Per-dataset inverse prevalence (BoolQ 11.3% down to MMLU-STEM 3.9%)

record.verdict_notes:
There are major internal inconsistencies:
- Inverse-subset means differ between sections: 66.1/41.5 vs 78.9/49.5, and a stated 39.9pp gap.
- The 405B model's score (41.5%) equals the large-group mean.
- Intervention model lists differ between Section 3.4 and B.2.4.
- The large-model cutoff is stated both as >70B and as ≥70B, yet Qwen2.5-32B is counted as large in the intervention.
- The paired test uses 96 of 115 items.

The inverse subset is selected on noisy per-problem greedy outputs, so regression to the mean may explain part of the brevity gains. Single author; preprint.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No loss curves fitted on small runs or predictions for larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute comparison or optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count and measure loss.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning scaling law, or transfer loss law is tested.
It tests benchmark accuracy against model size under selected prompt conditions, not predictability from pretraining loss or broad downstream scaling across tasks and training setups.
The study does not fit scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits, or compare how fitting choices change them.

rows.subject: Small-model aggregate (models ≤10B) versus large-model aggregate (models ≥70B)
rows.stage_stated: Mixed; evaluated models include instruct/chat and base models
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean accuracy by model-size group on the 115 problems classified as inverse-scaling problems under standard prompts.
rows.uncertainty: Cohen’s d = 1.34; Mann-Whitney U p < 0.001 for all datasets
rows.note: The larger size group scores lower on the selected inverse-scaling problems.
rows.check: Selection value. The 115 'inverse' problems are defined as those where small-model mean accuracy beats large-model mean by more than 5pp (B.1.4), so small > large on them holds by construction. This cannot count as a reversal of V6.

rows.subject: 31-model aggregate
rows.stage_stated: Mixed; evaluated models include instruct/chat and base models
rows.operation_detail: Correlated parameter count with accuracy on inverse-scaling problems.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between model size and accuracy
rows.note: The reported size-accuracy association is negative on these problems.
rows.check: The correlation is computed only on problems selected for small > large, so the negative sign is largely built in by selection. It is not an independent test of size versus accuracy.

rows.stage_stated: Mixed; evaluated models include instruct/chat and base models
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean accuracy by model-size group on problems classified as normal-scaling problems.
rows.note: This is the study’s reported normal-problem comparison.
rows.check: Selection value. 'Normal' problems are defined as large > small by more than 5pp, so the large-model advantage holds by construction. The appendix figures also conflict with Section 4.2.

rows.operation_detail: Measured benchmark accuracy under standard control prompts.

rows.operation_detail: Measured accuracy with a brief-response constraint.

relationships.condition: Problem-level accuracy, standard bare prompts, 31 models, five benchmarks
relationships.reason: From the text (Section 4.1), not from the rows: 715 problems scale normally and 115 (7.7%) favour small models by more than 5pp. Per-problem gains are therefore not uniform. Reversal magnitudes on the selected subset (R1, R2, R4) are selection artifacts.
relationships.display_finding: Although 715 problems improved with scale, 115 (7.7%) favored smaller models by more than five percentage points, with selected-subset reversal magnitudes affected by selection.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Larger models score lower than smaller ones on the reported inverse-problem aggregates, and size correlates negatively with accuracy (R1, R2, R4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard prompts on the reported normal-scaling problem subset and brief prompts on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM
reader_labels.reason: The larger group scores higher on normal-scaling problems, and the brief prompt reverses the size gap on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM (R3, R14, R15).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Selected intervention models across datasets and prompt conditions
reader_labels.reason: Effects depend on dataset and prompt: brief prompts leave small-model leads on ARC-Easy and CommonsenseQA, slightly widen the BoolQ gap, and direct-answer prompting lowers small-model accuracy substantially (R7–R13).
